PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Prohibits any new state tax (1) imposed on the ownership of personal property (all things people own other than real estate), or (2) that applies retroactively based on taxpayer’s past activities. Nullifies taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that conflict with this measure. Fiscal Impact: Possibility that tax revenues will not go up as much in the future. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; State Building & Construction Trades Council of CA; AMVETS Department of CA Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would continue to have the option to establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax retirement and savings—even though you already paid taxes on that money when you earned it! Prop. 42 protects Californians from this double taxation, by prohibiting new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement and savings. You earned it. Prop. 42 protects it.
CON
This is just another billionaire-funded trick. Prop. 42 isn’t really about protecting your retirement savings—its only real purpose is to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Vote NO on 42.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance

THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION

This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!

Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of
2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.

Constitution, to read:

## Prop. 42: The 401(k) decoy
Prop.
42 is pitched as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts, barring new state taxes on those assets and restricting certain retroactive taxes.
The editorial board describes it bluntly as a poison pill.
The suggestion that any governor would raid middle-class retirement accounts, the board writes, is implausible — any governor who tried “would soon be unemployed.”
Even the Legislature, which the board characterizes as inclined to spend more than it should, “knows not to mess with your 401(k).”
Opponents also note it appears to be an unsettled legal question whether retirement accounts can be taxed at all, because no government has tried.
Prop.
42 would embed its restrictions in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
The board argues it would create “the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property” while in fact restricting the state’s future tax options — until the next constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure altered that policy.
The real function is familiar: if Prop.
42 collects more “yes” votes than Prop.
40, the wealth tax does not take effect.
“Prop.
42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires,” the editorial board wrote.
“Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.”

# Taxing wealth is a dangerous step toward taxing retirement savings
...
By Chris HannanGuest contributor

...

This November, Californians have an opportunity to protect the hard-earned retirement savings they have earned.
For the workers I represent, retirement isn’t a windfall.
It’s earned across jobsites from thousands of hours worked, over decades of early mornings, long shifts and hard physical work.
We need to protect what we’ve saved — and that’s why I’m voting yes on Proposition 42.
Working people already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
They shouldn’t pay taxes on that money twice simply because it’s sitting in a retirement or savings account.
Proposition 42 prevents that double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new taxes to be imposed on retirement accounts, life savings and other personal property.

   - New taxes on the ownership or control of "retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — defined extremely broadly to include "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including, but not limited to, financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings, and other assets..."

   - Support: Southern California News Group (Daily News, OC Register), San Diego Union-Tribune

Opposed by California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Taxpayers Association, California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children's Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council.

Interesting — the firefighters and building trades, which support Prop 42, also oppose Prop 40. Newsom opposes Prop 40 and endorsed Prop 42.

- Locking in a prohibition prevents future misguided wealth taxes at the state level. State-level wealth taxes face serious problems: billionaires can move (Brin already did), and enforcement depends on federal info-sharing.
- The ban doesn't affect existing taxes; it only prohibits NEW taxes on ownership.

Arguments against:
- Permanently constraining the state's taxing options via constitution is bad governance; future generations should decide.
- It's a billionaire-backed ruse; passing it rewards deception and extreme spending disparities ($351M spent, 90% to defeat the wealth tax).
- Prop 40's revenues are earmarked for healthcare, addressing real needs (hospital closures, healthcare costs).
- The measure is broader than "retirement savings" — it covers ALL personal property, which could block reasonable future proposals.
- Retroactivity provisions could hamper emergency responses? No — it actually has emergency exceptions. But it does limit the state's ability to respond to fiscal emergencies with retroactive taxes... which most people would consider reasonable anyway.

Hmm. This is genuinely a values-laden choice. Many editorial boards across the spectrum say No because of the deceptive process. But there are also respected voices saying Yes (SCNG, SDUT) on policy grounds.

The most defensible recommendation, I think, weighs:
1. The measure's deceptive nature and its true purpose (killing Prop 40, which voters should decide on its own merits via Prop 40 vote).
2. The overbreadth (constitutionalizing a ban covering ALL personal property, not just retirement accounts).
3. The process criticism (poison pill, billionaire-funded).

A "No" vote keeps the Prop 40 question decided by the Prop 40 vote itself, rather than by a decoy measure. If the user opposes Prop 40, they can vote No on Prop 40 directly. Voting Yes on 42 lets a decoy measure do that work while also permanently constraining the state.

But wait — there's a strategic consideration: if the user supports the billionaire tax, voting No on 42 is essential. If the user opposes the billionaire tax, voting Yes on 42 both kills Prop 40 (if 42 gets more votes) AND prevents future wealth taxes. But they could also just vote No on Prop 40, though that only defeats it this cycle, and a future wealth tax could come back.

The user asked me to research and decide. I don't know the user's politics. I should make a judgment based on the merits. Let me look at the strongest analyses on each side, then decide.

My inclination: The deceptiveness and overbreadth are strong reasons to vote No. Editorial consensus across the spectrum (Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee/McClatchy, LA Times' Skelton) leans No. Also, I think it's bad policy to permanently constitutionalize a broad tax prohibition — it reduces democratic flexibility for future generations. And the fact that it's funded by billionaires specifically to defeat a measure taxing themselves, while marketed as protecting ordinary retirement savers, is exactly the kind of initiative abuse that should be discouraged.

Counter: If I think wealth taxes are bad policy (many economists do), then Yes locks that in. But the right way to oppose Prop 40 is to vote No on Prop 40 — on honest grounds — not to pass a decoy. Also note: the same billionaires spent $118.5M opposing Prop 40 directly. So there's already a direct channel for opposition.

Also the emergency exception carve-out: retroactive taxes allowed only for Governor-declared emergencies/fiscal emergencies with revenues limited to response. And the definition of "tax" references Article XIII A Section 3(b) definition — taxes vs. fees.

Another consideration: Prop 42's Section 1 prohibits taxes on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — and "personal savings" is defined to include ALL personal property. This is much broader than the ballot summary suggests ("Prohibits new state personal property taxes"). It would ban, e.g., future taxes on ownership of luxury goods, art, yachts? (art collections, yachts are personal property) — so a future luxury tax on yachts/jets might be unconstitutional. It also bans taxing business interests ownership (a tax on holding shares). Some might say that's exactly the point (blocking wealth taxes), but it also forecloses narrow, targeted taxes.

Let me do a bit more research on:
1. The Stanford study on Prop 40's cost ($39B loss claim)
2. Prop 40's actual provisions (exclusions for pensions/retirement accounts, exit taxes, etc.)
3. What happened with the "six proposals to tax retirement and savings" claim
4. Maybe polling

Then I'll decide. Let me also check the LA Times detailed guide to Prop 42 and Prop 40's analysis.","format":"unknown","index":0}]

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.

California (https://www.latimes.com/california)

Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. Now I have a comprehensive view of the text of Prop 42. Key observations:

1. Prop 42 (the "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of 2026") adds Article VIII to the California Constitution prohibiting:
   - New taxes on the ownership or control of "retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — defined extremely broadly to include "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including, but not limited to, financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings, and other assets..."
   - Retroactive taxes (with exceptions for emergencies declared by the Governor, where tax revenues are limited to responding to the emergency, and only up to 365 days retroactively)

2. It has a "conflicting measures" clause: If Prop 42 receives more yes votes than a conflicting measure (i.e., Prop 40), the other measure is null and void.

3. The definition is sweeping — "all personal property, whether tangible or intangible" — this would ban the state from ever imposing any tax on ownership of basically anything except real estate. Note that existing taxes (like the vehicle license fee and business personal property taxes) are grandfathered in since they were in effect before Dec 31, 2025.

4. The measure was funded by Sergey Brin (~$102M+) through "Building a Better California" — the same group opposing Prop 40.

5. Editorials: 
   - Support: Southern California News Group (Daily News, OC Register), San Diego Union-Tribune
   - Oppose: Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee (McClatchy), LA Times' George Skelton ("Twin poison pills... No.")

6. Prop 40 itself: 5% one-time wealth tax on billionaires (assets > $1B), revenue primarily for healthcare. Supported by Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW. Opposed by California Primary Care Association, California School Boards Association, California Taxpayers Association, California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children's Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building & Construction Trades Council.

Interesting — the firefighters and building trades, which support Prop 42, also oppose Prop 40. Newsom opposes Prop 40 and endorsed Prop 42.

The instruction says I can only answer yes or no — so my final answer should be either "Yes" or "No" (presumably with reasoning leading up to it, or maybe just the single word). So the expected output format is probably: research, then a final answer of "Yes" or "No."

Let me think about how to decide this. I should weigh:

Arguments FOR Prop 42 (Yes):
- Protects retirement savings from potential future state taxation on asset ownership
- Prohibits retroactive taxation, which is generally viewed as unfair
- Prevents double taxation
- Supported by firefighters, building trades unions, AMVETS, seniors groups
- Governor Newsom endorsed it
- Restrains state's taxing power broadly
- Even opponents (Mercury News) said if it had limited itself to nullifying Prop 40 they could have supported it — no wait, they said if it had limited itself to nullifying Prop 40 they could have supported it. Hmm, actually the Mercury News said: "If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it" — that means they oppose it because it's too broad, not because nullifying Prop 40 is bad. Interesting nuance.

Arguments AGAINST Prop 42 (No):
- It's a billionaire-funded (Sergey Brin, $100M+) countermeasure designed to nullify Prop 40 (the billionaire tax), deceivingly framed as protecting ordinary retirement accounts
- The claim that the state is coming for your 401(k) is fear-mongering; no such proposal exists for ordinary retirement accounts; Prop 40 explicitly excludes qualified pensions and retirement accounts from "assets"
- It would permanently embed in the Constitution a sweeping ban on any future wealth tax — including more moderate proposals (e.g., Newsom's proposed national minimum tax on >$100M wealth; a California version could never happen)
- The definition of "personal savings" is extremely broad — all personal property tangible or intangible — which could have unforeseen consequences for future tax policy flexibility
- The emergency exception: retroactive taxes allowed within 365 days for Governor-declared emergencies with revenue limited to emergency response — this could constrain the state in fiscal crises
- Deceptive ballot-measure games: poison pill measures like this are criticized by editorial boards across the spectrum
- It could reduce future revenue flexibility

The pros/cons here involve values: do you favor wealth taxes on billionaires? Do you favor locking tax policy into the Constitution?

1. Policy substance: Is a permanent constitutional ban on wealth taxes/property-ownership taxes good policy? Most tax policy experts (including many who oppose Prop 40 on merits) consider constitutionalizing broad tax prohibitions bad governance — it locks in policy and prevents future legislatures from responding. Both conservative and liberal editorial boards oppose the games-playing here. The Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee all say No. Southern California News Group and SD Union-Tribune say Yes.

2. Process: Prop 42 is a "poison pill" designed by billionaires to kill Prop 40. That's a deceptive use of the initiative process. Even George Skelton (LA Times, who dislikes Prop 40) says No on 41/42 because of the deceptive games-playing.

3. Deceptive framing: The "protect your 401(k)" framing is misleading — no proposal exists to tax ordinary retirement accounts, and Prop 40 explicitly excludes them. The claim of "six proposals to tax retirement and savings" seems to refer to wealth tax proposals aimed at the ultra-wealthy.

4. Retroactivity ban: On its own merits, a ban on retroactive taxation has some appeal — retroactive taxes are generally considered unfair. But Prop 40's "retroactive" element is about billionaires who were residents on Jan 1, 2026 (before the election). Some view that as unfair targeting of people who already left the state (like Brin, who moved to Nevada in late 2025 — wait, he moved in late 2025, before Jan 1, 2026, so he wouldn't be covered? Actually, let me think about what matters most:

The core question: Should the California Constitution permanently prohibit new state taxes on the ownership of personal property (all things other than real estate), including financial assets, and prohibit most retroactive taxes?

Arguments in favor of this being good policy:
- Wealth taxes are widely criticized by economists (capital flight, avoidance, administrative difficulty). Prop 40 itself is flawed — a Stanford study says it could cost the state $39 billion (need to check that). Even Newsom opposes it and favors a national approach.
- Locking in a prohibition prevents future misguided wealth taxes at the state level. State-level wealth taxes face serious problems: billionaires can move (Brin already did), and enforcement depends on federal info-sharing.
- The ban doesn't affect existing taxes; it only prohibits NEW taxes on ownership.

Arguments against:
- Permanently constraining the state's taxing options via constitution is bad governance; future generations should decide.
- It's a billionaire-backed ruse; passing it rewards deception and extreme spending disparities ($351M spent, 90% to defeat the wealth tax).

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic and disincentivize its further use by voting no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
