Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic and disincentivize its further use by voting no.

About (https://igs.berkeley.edu/about)
IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. Our core mission remains promoting interdisciplinary research with a principal focus on American and California governance, politics, and policy. We bring together faculty members and students from across the Berkeley campus with an interdisciplinary focus not easily replicated by a single department

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
November 3, 2026 General Election Ballot Endorsements
For each election, staff at the IGS Library compile endorsements from key state newspapers, non-profit organizations, political parties, and unions. For the November election, we begin checking websites for endorsements in mid-September and continue checking weekly until Election Day.
Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.
Newspapers
Many newspapers require a subscription. Whenever possible, we link to a freely available version online. In other cases, we search Access World News, a UCB licensed database, to identify and link to endorsements. A current CalNet ID and password is required to access the articles.

I've now got a thorough picture: the official analysis and full legal text, the Prop 40 relationship, the funding, the dueling economic studies, editorial positions, and polling. Here's what my research turned up, and my decision.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Prop 42 ("Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act") would amend the California Constitution to (1) ban any new state tax on the *ownership* of personal property, and (2) ban most retroactive taxes. On its face, that sounds like protecting 401(k)s from double taxation. But the fine print reveals a much bigger story:

**It's a "poison pill" targeting Prop 40.** Prop 42 contains an explicit clause nullifying Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on ~200 billionaires, earmarked for healthcare) if Prop 42 gets more yes votes. It was placed on the ballot by "Building a Better California," a PAC funded by ~$102M+ from Google co-founder Sergey Brin — one of the billionaires Prop 40 would tax. Brin's group has spent $300M+ across the three measures, outspending supporters 9-to-1 in one of the most expensive ballot fights in California history.

**The retirement-savings pitch is largely fear-mongering.** No proposal exists to tax ordinary 401(k)s, pensions, or savings accounts. Prop 40 *explicitly excludes* qualified pensions and retirement accounts from its definition of taxable assets. All six prior wealth-tax bills in the Legislature died without passing. California taxes retirement funds on withdrawal, following federal rules — nobody is "coming for your retirement."

**The ban is far broader than advertised.** "Personal savings" is legally defined to include *all* personal property — stocks, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, yachts, art. This would permanently constitutionalize a ban on essentially any future asset/wealth tax, no matter how narrowly targeted or well-designed, locking today's policy into the constitution for future generations.

## What the experts say

- **Editorial boards:** Nearly every major board says No — SF Chronicle ("just another poison-pill measure... reject this appalling tactic"), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee ("the 401(k) decoy... a poison pill"), and LA Times' veteran columnist George Skelton (who dislikes Prop 40 but calls 41/42 "twin poison pills"). Only the more conservative SD Union-Tribune and Southern California News Group say Yes.
- **Economists are split on Prop 40 itself** (Zucman/Saez: ~$100B raised; Stanford's Rauh/Jaros: possible net loss due to billionaire exodus) — but even most Prop 40 skeptics say the right way to oppose it is a straight "No on 40," not this decoy.
- **Polling** shows the race tightening, with many voters unaware the measures are designed as poison pills.

## Why this matters for your vote

The core problem isn't wealth-tax policy — reasonable people disagree there, and you can vote on Prop 40 directly. The problem is that Prop 42 is deception baked into the constitution: a measure funded and drafted by the people it protects, marketed to ordinary savers with threats that don't exist, whose real function is to cancel a separate measure voters are deciding on its own merits, while permanently stripping future voters of tax options through an overbroad constitutional lock-in. Even Gov. Newsom's endorsement doesn't cure the measure's structural dishonesty — and passing it rewards and encourages this exact playbook.

## My answer

**No.**

If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote No on Prop 40 directly — that's the honest way to defeat it. A Yes on 42 means letting a billionaire-funded decoy do that work while permanently constitutionalizing a sweeping ban that reaches far beyond retirement accounts.

- Protecting against a future tax on savings = "double taxation" — but unrealized appreciation has never been taxed; wealth taxes aren't double taxation in that sense.
- The retroactivity issue: Prop 40's tax hits billionaires resident as of Jan 1, 2026, including those who left mid-year (e.g., "billionaire was resident Jan 1, then moved"). Some see that as unfair — taxing people who left. That's the strongest fairness argument against Prop 40's design. But Prop 40 only covers those who were residents on Jan 1, 2026 — people who had not yet had the chance to react to a law that wasn't passed. Retroactivity concerns are real here. However, the remedy for that is voting No on Prop 40, not passing a decoy constitutional amendment that also bans ALL future asset taxes.

I've now got a thorough picture: the official analysis and full legal text, the Prop 40 relationship, the funding, the dueling economic studies, editorial positions, and polling. Here's what my research turned up, and my decision.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Prop 42 ("Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act") would amend the California Constitution to (1) ban any new state tax on the *ownership* of personal property, and (2) ban most retroactive taxes. On its face, that sounds like protecting 401(k)s from double taxation. But the fine print reveals a much bigger story:

**It's a "poison pill" targeting Prop 40.** Prop 42 contains an explicit clause nullifying Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on ~200 billionaires, earmarked for healthcare) if Prop 42 gets more yes votes. It was placed on the ballot by "Building a Better California," a PAC funded by ~$102M+ from Google co-founder Sergey Brin — one of the billionaires Prop 40 would tax. Brin's group has spent $300M+ across the three measures, outspending supporters 9-to-1 in one of the most expensive ballot fights in California history.

**The retirement-savings pitch is largely fear-mongering.** No proposal exists to tax ordinary 401(k)s, pensions, or savings accounts. Prop 40 *explicitly excludes* qualified pensions and retirement accounts from its definition of taxable assets. All six prior wealth-tax bills in the Legislature died without passing. California taxes retirement funds on withdrawal, following federal rules — nobody is "coming for your retirement."

**The ban is far broader than advertised.** "Personal savings" is legally defined to include *all* personal property — stocks, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, yachts, art. This would permanently constitutionalize a ban on essentially any future asset/wealth tax, no matter how narrowly targeted or well-designed, locking today's policy into the constitution for future generations.

## What the experts say

- **Editorial boards:** Nearly every major board says No — SF Chronicle ("just another poison-pill measure... reject this appalling tactic"), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee ("the 401(k) decoy... a poison pill"), and LA Times' veteran columnist George Skelton (who dislikes Prop 40 but calls 41/42 "twin poison pills"). Only the more conservative SD Union-Tribune and Southern California News Group say Yes.
- **Economists are split on Prop 40 itself** (Zucman/Saez: ~$100B raised; Stanford's Rauh/Jaros: possible net loss due to billionaire exodus) — but even most Prop 40 skeptics say the right way to oppose it is a straight "No on 40," not this decoy.
- **Polling** shows the race tightening, with many voters unaware the measures are designed as poison pills.

## Why this matters for your vote

The core problem isn't wealth-tax policy — reasonable people disagree there, and you can vote on Prop 40 directly. The problem is that Prop 42 is deception baked into the constitution: a measure funded and drafted by the people it protects, marketed to ordinary savers with threats that don't exist, whose real function is to cancel a separate measure voters are deciding on its own merits, while permanently stripping future voters of tax options through an overbroad constitutional lock-in. Even Gov. Newsom's endorsement doesn't cure the measure's structural dishonesty — and passing it rewards and encourages this exact playbook.

## My answer

**No.**

If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote No on Prop 40 directly — that's the honest way to defeat it. A Yes on 42 means letting a billionaire-funded decoy do that work while permanently constitutionalizing a sweeping ban that reaches far beyond retirement accounts.

PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.

CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION

WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.

Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

YES

NO

# Taxing wealth is a dangerous step toward taxing retirement savings
...
By Chris HannanGuest contributor
Oct. 29, 2026 4:13 PM PT
...
- 3 min
...
This November, Californians have an opportunity to protect the hard-earned retirement savings they have earned.
For the workers I represent, retirement isn’t a windfall.
It’s earned across jobsites from thousands of hours worked, over decades of early mornings, long shifts and hard physical work.
We need to protect what we’ve saved — and that’s why I’m voting yes on Proposition 42.
Working people already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
They shouldn’t pay taxes on that money twice simply because it’s sitting in a retirement or savings account.
Proposition 42 prevents that double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows new taxes to be imposed on retirement accounts, life savings and other personal property.
...

- The column argues that retirement savings represent decades of work, not a windfall, and that workers should be able to count on those savings when they retire.
- It supports Proposition 42 as protection against new state taxes on financial assets and personal property.
The article frames such taxes as double taxation because workers have already paid income taxes on the money they saved.^[2]^^[6]^

## Prop. 42: The 401(k) decoy
Prop.
42 is pitched as a safeguard for personal property and 401(k) accounts, barring new state taxes on those assets and restricting certain retroactive taxes.
The editorial board describes it bluntly as a poison pill.
The suggestion that any governor would raid middle-class retirement accounts, the board writes, is implausible — any governor who tried “would soon be unemployed.”
Even the Legislature, which the board characterizes as inclined to spend more than it should, “knows not to mess with your 401(k).”
Opponents also note it appears to be an unsettled legal question whether retirement accounts can be taxed at all, because no government has tried.
Prop.
42 would embed its restrictions in the California Constitution, leaving voters as the only route to change them.
The board argues it would create “the illusion of permanently settling California tax policy on financial assets and other personal property” while in fact restricting the state’s future tax options — until the next constitutional amendment or competing voter-approved measure altered that policy.
The real function is familiar: if Prop.
42 collects more “yes” votes than Prop.
40, the wealth tax does not take effect.
“Prop.
42 is a poison pill designed to derail the real debate over a one-time wealth tax on billionaires,” the editorial board wrote.
“Voters should reject the decoy and vote no.”

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> The so-called billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide) has become one of the most contested California propositions in years, generating national interest and massive spending by opponents (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax). It also has spawned two rival ballot measures (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
Here’s a cheat sheet for sorting it all out.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Voter guide to the 2026 California general election (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-general-election-voter-guide)
Oct. 1, 2026
Proposition 40
The basics
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets. The tax applies to people with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in California on Jan. 1.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-40-billionaire-tax-voter-guide)
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
Ninety percent of the tax would fund healthcare, and 10% would go toward education and food assistance.
Advertisement
The tax would affect hundreds of billionaires whose net worth includes assets such as their businesses, stocks and other investments. Real property, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded.
Proposition 41
It’s called the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness and Efficiency in California Government Act. But it is deeply connected to Proposition 40 and is funded by foes of the billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-01-19/explaining-californias-billionaire-tax-proposals-backlash-exodus).
The basics
Proposition 41 requires the state auditor to review programs funded by proposed special taxes before they appear on the ballot. More importantly, it also prohibits new state taxes from being exempted from a voter-approved state spending limit.
Advertisement
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 41: Special tax audit proposal could block billionaire tax (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-41-tax-audit-voter-guide)
Prop 41 would require audits for new state special taxes and prohibit certain new state taxes. It also could nullify the billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says passage of Proposition 41 could prevent Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, from becoming law even if voters approve it. This could happen if Proposition 41 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 would limit the state’s ability to impose certain new taxes. But it’s more complicated and far-reaching than that description might sound. And, yes, it’s also backed by opponents of Proposition 40.
The basics
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on “retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings” that take effect after Jan. 1, 2026. It also would bar retroactive taxes on past earnings unless the state is using revenue from the tax to respond to emergencies such as a fire or a flood.
California (https://www.latimes.com/california)
Your guide to Proposition 42: Tax ban on retirement, personal savings (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-42-tax-ban-retirement-savings-voter-guide)
Prop 42 would ban new taxes on various forms of personal savings and certain retroactive taxes and also could block a proposed billionaire tax.
Oct. 1, 2026
Impact
The Legislative Analyst’s Office says Proposition 42 could nullify Proposition 40 because the two measures conflict with each other. If voters approve both, the one with the most “yes” votes generally would become law, the office says.
Dig deeper
The billionaire tax was pushed by the Service Employees International Union (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-26/powerful-union-billionaire-tax-alleged-bargaining-chip)-United Healthcare Workers West and has some labor and progressive support (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-02/california-democratic-party-endorses-prop-40-billionaire-tax), including from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the state Democratic Party. They say the tax is needed to help the less fortunate and that the super-rich can afford it. But key Democrats and some key unions are not supporting it.
Critics include some ofCalifornia’s richest people, (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-17/billionaires-open-purse-to-fight-california-wealth-tax) and they are spending a fortune to defeat it. They say it will hurt innovation and drive the wealthy out of the state, hurting the treasury.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic and disincentivize its further use by voting no.

0
Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$

content.text:
I've now got a thorough picture: the official analysis and full legal text, the Prop 40 relationship, the funding, the dueling economic studies, editorial positions, and polling. Here's what my research turned up, and my decision.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Prop 42 ("Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act") would amend the California Constitution to (1) ban any new state tax on the *ownership* of personal property, and (2) ban most retroactive taxes. On its face, that sounds like protecting 401(k)s from double taxation. But the fine print reveals a much bigger story:

**It's a "poison pill" targeting Prop 40.** Prop 42 contains an explicit clause nullifying Prop 40 (the one-time 5% tax on ~200 billionaires, earmarked for healthcare) if Prop 42 gets more yes votes. It was placed on the ballot by "Building a Better California," a PAC funded by ~$102M+ from Google co-founder Sergey Brin — one of the billionaires Prop 40 would tax. Brin's group has spent $300M+ across the three measures, outspending supporters 9-to-1 in one of the most expensive ballot fights in California history.

**The retirement-savings pitch is largely fear-mongering.** No proposal exists to tax ordinary 401(k)s, pensions, or savings accounts. Prop 40 *explicitly excludes* qualified pensions and retirement accounts from its definition of taxable assets. All six prior wealth-tax bills in the Legislature died without passing. California taxes retirement funds on withdrawal, following federal rules — nobody is "coming for your retirement."

**The ban is far broader than advertised.** "Personal savings" is legally defined to include *all* personal property — stocks, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, yachts, art. This would permanently constitutionalize a ban on essentially any future asset/wealth tax, no matter how narrowly targeted or well-designed, locking today's policy into the constitution for future generations.

## What the experts say

- **Editorial boards:** Nearly every major board says No — SF Chronicle ("just another poison-pill measure... reject this appalling tactic"), Mercury News/East Bay Times, Sacramento Bee ("the 401(k) decoy... a poison pill"), and LA Times' veteran columnist George Skelton (who dislikes Prop 40 but calls 41/42 "twin poison pills"). Only the more conservative SD Union-Tribune and Southern California News Group say Yes.
- **Economists are split on Prop 40 itself** (Zucman/Saez: ~$100B raised; Stanford's Rauh/Jaros: possible net loss due to billionaire exodus) — but even most Prop 40 skeptics say the right way to oppose it is a straight "No on 40," not this decoy.
- **Polling** shows the race tightening, with many voters unaware the measures are designed as poison pills.

## Why this matters for your vote

The core problem isn't wealth-tax policy — reasonable people disagree there, and you can vote on Prop 40 directly. The problem is that Prop 42 is deception baked into the constitution: a measure funded and drafted by the people it protects, marketed to ordinary savers with threats that don't exist, whose real function is to cancel a separate measure voters are deciding on its own merits, while permanently stripping future voters of tax options through an overbroad constitutional lock-in. Even Gov. Newsom's endorsement doesn't cure the measure's structural dishonesty — and passing it rewards and encourages this exact playbook.

## My answer

**No.**

If you oppose the billionaire tax, vote No on Prop 40 directly — that's the honest way to defeat it. A Yes on 42 means letting a billionaire-funded decoy do that work while permanently constitutionalizing a sweeping ban that reaches far beyond retirement accounts.
